Hiệu năng chạy các container Docker bên trong unkernel cụ thể ra sao dù nhân hỗ trợ namespaces và cgroups?
Cách tự dựng và cấu hình một Wisp server riêng cho unkernel chi tiết như thế nào?

## pithings/unkernel (https://github.com/pithings/unkernel)
Description: A real Linux kernel, compiled to WebAssembly. It boots to a shell in less than a second.
Homepage: https://unkernel.dev
Language: TypeScript; license: GPL-2.0; created 2026-11-12; last push 2026-11-22
Latest release: v0.2.0-261122-4e58555 (2026-11-22)
README (start):
**A real Linux kernel, compiled to WebAssembly. It boots to a shell in less than a second.**

  Try it ·
  Performance ·
  Features ·
  CLI ·
  How it works ·
  Benchmarks ·
  JavaScript SDK

unkernel is Linux 7.x built as a single wasm module with a real MMU. The
kernel (syscalls, scheduler, memory management, ext4, TCP/IP) is compiled
code, not emulated, so programs get Linux's own behavior down to the edge
cases. Only user programs are emulated: unmodified aarch64 (arm64) Linux
binaries, so Alpine and Debian packages run as they are.

[Open a page](#-try-it-in-the-browser) and you have a Linux machine with a
shell, a package manager, a persistent disk, internet access, and a screen
with sound. It runs entirely on your device, with nothing to install and no
server, and every layer is open source. [How it works](#-how-it-works)
explains the design.

  

## ⚡ Performance

Much of what makes a system feel slow lives in the kernel: starting
processes, syscalls, page faults, file and network I/O. In unkernel that
path runs at wasm speed.

- **Boot**: the kernel reaches `/init` about 70 ms after it starts, and the Alpine
  prompt appears 0.3 s after `node` launches. The page downloads about
  10 MB, and Alpine boots in 48 MiB of guest memory.
- **Syscalls at close to native cost**: `getppid` takes about 170 ns (110
  native, 1.7 µs under qemu-system), a 64-byte `read` about 170 ns (160
  native).
- **fork at native speed**: fork + exit + wait takes about 60 µs, against
  about 70 µs natively and 1.2 ms under qemu-system.
- **A JIT for user code**: hot aarch64 code, including the AES, PMULL and
  SHA instructions OpenSSL uses, is compiled to wasm while it runs. With
  it a shell loop runs 1.6 times and `sort` 2.3 times as fast as on the
  interpreter alone, and OpenSSL in the guest does AES-128-GCM at about
  100 MB/s and SHA-256 at about 160 MB/s.

The syscall and fork numbers were measured on 2026-11-14 (with the
riscv64 user space the project started with; the path through the kernel
is the same), the JIT numbers on 2026-11-18. CPU-heavy programs are well
behind native: `apk search` over the main index takes about 0.8 s, `apk
add python3` about 3.4 s. [Benchmarks](#-benchmarks) has the full numbers.

## 🐧 A real kernel

Anything a program relies on, from `/proc` and `epoll` to cgroups and
overlayfs, behaves as it does on a server, because it runs the same code.

- **A real MMU** (`arch/wasm` with Sv39 page tables): `fork`, `mmap`,
  copy-on-write, shared memory, threads and signals behave as they do on
  hardware. This is not a NOMMU port where programs are limited to `vfork`.
- **Linux's own file systems**: ext4, overlayfs, tmpfs, loop devices, FUSE,
  and 9p, which [mounts file systems](#mount-host-files) your program serves
  from the host. The root file system is an overlay: a read-only distro
  image under your changes, which go to a persistent ext4 disk, so
  everything you change survives a reload, and a safe mode recovers a
  system you broke.
- **Linux's own TCP/IP stack**, with DHCP and DNS, reaching the internet
  through your host's sockets or a Wisp proxy
  ([Add a network](#add-a-network)).
- **cgroups, namespaces, userfaultfd, fanotify and TUN**: enough for
  systemd to boot Ubuntu 26.10 to `multi-user.target`.
- **Devices**: a [framebuffer (`/dev/fb0`), evdev keyboard, mouse and touch,
  sound through ALSA and `/dev/dsp`](#display-input-and-sound),
  [AF_VSOCK](#talk-over-vsock), and [shared memory](#share-memory) with the
  host.
- **aarch64 user space**: ARMv8.0-A with FP and AdvSIMD plus the AES,
  PMULL, SHA1, SHA2, SHA512, SHA3, CRC32 and LSE atomics extensions, so
  distribution binaries and
  OpenSSL's hardware AES, GHASH and SHA paths run unchanged. aarch64 is a
  first-class port of
  every distribution, so their full, current package archives are
  available.

[Known limits](#-known-limits) lists what is still missing.

## 🧰 What you can do with it

- **[Carry a Linux shell anywhere](#-try-it-in-the-browser).** Alpine Linux
  3.24 runs in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, including on phones. Install
  anything with `apk add` from Alpine's regular mirrors. Type a command that
  isn't installed, such as `htop`, and its package is installed for you. apk
  starts with only the `main` repository, because it is about 4x faster that
  way; `community` is added the first time a command needs it.
- **Run real runtimes and tools**: Node and npm, Python, OpenSSL, curl and
  `wget`, straight from the distribution. Debian 13 boots the same way as
  Alpine (`--distro debian`), with apt.
- **[Write graphics and sound programs](#display-input-and-sound)** against
  `/dev/fb0`, evdev and ALSA. Try `glimmer`, a tiny game with sound.
- **[Embed Linux in your app](#-use-it-from-javascript)** with a
  zero-dependency TypeScript SDK, published as
  [`unkernel`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/unkernel). The same kernel file
  runs in Node and in every supported browser, optionally [in a
  worker](#run-it-in-a-worker). [Disks](#add-disks) can be local ext4 images,
  http(s) images fetched by range, or a persistent disk in IndexedDB. The SDK
  is MIT-licensed, and there is no closed engine or license key behind it, so
  you can ship it in your product and host it wherever you like.
- **Talk to the guest** through [terminal sessions](#run-programs), each
  with its own pty and shell, [host directories and in-memory file
  systems](#mount-host-files) mounted in the guest, [vsock byte
  streams](#talk-over-vsock) and [zero-copy shared memory](#share-memory),
  with no network in between.
- **Script and test**: [the CLI](#-run-it-from-the-terminal) types input on a
  schedule, stops on a timeout, and reports how the guest ended in its exit
  code.

## 🌐 Try it in the browser

Open **[unkernel.dev](https://unkernel.dev/)**. A desktop appears after a
download of about 10 MB, with a shell in its Terminal window. Your changes
are saved in the browser. The Dock opens the apps (so do ⌘K on a Mac and
Ctrl-Shift-O elsewhere); Settings has the options and export or reset for
your disk, System the diagnostics. Ctrl-A n (or ⌘A n on a Mac) or `+` on
a Terminal window's tabs opens another terminal with its own shell, up to
9; Ctrl-A and a digit switches, and Ctrl-A ? lists every shortcut. The
wallpaper is a random photo from [Lorem Picsum](https://picsum.photos/)
by default, so the page fetches one from picsum.photos on every load;
the built-in wallpaper or a preset (Settings > Desktop) stops that.

The page takes a few URL parameters:

| Parameter | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `?mem=512` | Guest memory in MiB |
| `?append=...` | Extra kernel command line |
| `?net=0` | Boot without a network |
| `?wisp=wss://...` | Use your own [Wisp](https://github.com/MercuryWorkshop/wisp-protocol) proxy |
| `?jit=0` | Interpreter only |
| `?data=0` | No persistent disk, a fresh system every time |
| `?worker=0` | Run the kernel on the page's thread (default: in a Web Worker where the page is cross-origin isolated) |
| `?cpus=2` | Boot on that many CPUs, each in a Web Worker (default: half the device's threads, up to 4 on desktops and 2 in Firefox, one on phones, in Safari and on iOS, where the page has the SMP kernel and is cross-origin isolated; `?cpus=1`: one CPU) |
| `?gl=0` | No guest GL (on by default on Debian: the guest's Mesa renders through your browser's WebGL2, see below) |

On Debian the guest gets a GPU (`/dev/dri`, Settings, Guest GL): Mesa's
virgl driver draws through your browser's WebGL2. The renderer behind it
is downloaded only when a guest program first uses GL; the Guest GL row
in System > Environment then names the GPU (a software renderer such as SwiftShader
is flagged). Mesa is installed in the guest, not shipped:

```sh
sudo apt-get install -y mesa-utils libegl-mesa0 libgles2 kmscube
eglinfo -B -p gbm                 # OpenGL ES renderer: virgl ()
kmscube                           # on the display (Enter ends it)
sudo apt-get install -y xvfb xauth glmark2-es2-x11
xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 640x480x24" glmark2-es2   # frame rates
```

Wayland apps show as windows on the page: `wland foot` (or the
launcher's foot tile) starts wland's relay in the guest and runs the app
against it; [wland](https://github.com/pithings/wland)'s compositor runs in
the page and reads the app's pixels straight from guest memory. Each app
window is a window of the page's desktop; Ctrl-A w switches between them
and the other windows.

```sh
sudo apt-get install -y foot fonts-dejavu-core
wland foot
```

Browsers can't open raw TCP sockets, so the page reaches the internet
through a Wisp proxy. The default one accepts only known origins, so if you
host the page somewhere else, point `?wisp=` at your own proxy.

| Browser | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Chrome / Edge 137+ (desktop and Android) | ✅ works |
| Firefox 153+ | ✅ works |
| Safari 27+ on macOS, any browser on iOS/iPadOS 27 | ✅ works |
| Anything without [JSPI](#-how-it-works) | the page tells you what's missing |

## 💻 Run it from the terminal

```sh
npx unkernel
```

This boots Alpine, with networking over your host's sockets. Press
**Ctrl-]** to quit. The package holds the kernel and a small base system;
the first run downloads the Alpine image (about 4 MB) from the GitHub
release of your version and keeps it in `~/.cache/unkernel`.

```sh
npx unkernel --distro debian                 # Debian 13 instead (about 57 MB, downloaded once)
npx unkernel --distro none                   # no distro: the base shell (busybox)
npx unkernel --data my-data.img              # changes persist on a /data disk, created on first use
npx unkernel --display --sound               # a framebuffer and a sound card
npx unkernel --mem 1024 --no-net             # more memory, no network
npx unkernel --mount .:/work                 # this directory at /work in the guest (:ro for read-only)
npx unkernel --forward 8000:80               # host 127.0.0.1:8000 to port 80 in the guest
npx unkernel --timeout 60 --input '{8}uname -a\n{2}poweroff\n'   # scripted: wait, type, wait, type
npx unkernel --help                          # everything else
```

Without `--data`, changes to the root file system are kept in memory and
gone at exit; with it, each distro keeps its own in `/data/distros//`.
`--distro` also takes an image file or an http(s) URL, and
`UNKERNEL_CACHE_DIR` moves the download cache.

Exit codes: 0 power off, 1 halt or boot failure, 2 restart, 124 timeout, 253
kernel panic, 254 wasm trap, 255 fatal error. The CLI is built on the
[JavaScript SDK](#-use-it-from-javascript): `--mount` uses its [host
mounts](#mount-host-files) and `--forward` its
[`vm.connect()`](#talk-over-vsock).

## 🔍 How it works

Most "Linux in the browser" projects take one of three approaches:

- **Emulate a whole PC**, kernel included. This is faithful but slow,
  because every syscall and page fault goes through emulated hardware.
- **Emulate the CPU and reimplement the syscalls.** Programs run on an
  emulated CPU, often with a JIT, and a runtime answers their syscalls, with
  no Linux kernel at all. This is fast, but it covers only as much of Linux
  as the runtime implements.
- **Compile programs to wasm**, and run them on a kernel without an MMU or
  on a runtime that provides POSIX calls. This is fast, but native programs
  have to be rebuilt, and `fork` and anything else that needs an MMU breaks
  or is approximated.

unkernel keeps the best of each: the real Linux kernel, running at native
wasm speed, under unmodified binaries with a real MMU.

| Approach | Kernel | User space | MMU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whole-machine emulators (v86, JSLinux, container2wasm, QEMU's wasm build) | Linux, emulated | unmodified, emulated | emulated |
| Syscall emulators | none: a runtime reimplements the syscalls | unmodified, emulated | the runtime's own |
| POSIX runtimes for wasm (Wasmer WASIX, WebContainers, BrowserPod) | none: a runtime provides the syscalls | rebuilt for wasm, or JavaScript | none |

Wisp Protocol

Wisp is designed to be a low-overhead, easy to implement protocol for proxying multiple TCP and UDP sockets over a single websocket connection.

For the protocol specifications, see protocol.md.

Major Versions:

There are two major versions of Wisp:

Wisp V1 - The simpler version which is easier to implement, but without advanced features such as authentication.
Wisp V2 - Adds a handshake step which allows for adding protocol extensions, password and key authentication, MOTD messages, and more.
Client Implementations:
wisp-js/client - by @ading2210
epoxy-tls (Rust) - by @r58Playz
Server Implementations:
wisp-js/server - by @ading2210
epoxy-server (Rust) - by @r58Playz
wisp-server-python - by @ading2210
Woeful (C++) - by @FoxMoss
wisp-server-workers - by @r58Playz
Library Implementations:
wisp-js - by @ading2210
wisp-mux (Rust) - by @r58Playz
Software Using Wisp:
WispMark - A benchmarking tool for Wisp protocol implementations.
libcurl.js - A port of libcurl to WebAssembly, for proxying HTTPS requests from the browser with full TLS encryption
epoxy-tls - An encrypted proxy for browser javascript, written in Rust.
Wasmer SDK - A WebAssembly sandbox based on WASIX that runs software from the Wasmer registry.
Scramjet - An experimental web proxy that aims to be the successor to Ultraviolet.
Whisper - A client for Wisp that exposes the connection over a TUN device.
v86 - x86 PC emulator and x86-to-wasm JIT, running in the browser
Puter - An advanced, open-source internet operating system designed to be feature-rich, exceptionally fast, and highly extensible
browser.js - A browser environment for the web, based on Scramjet.
Wispcraft - A mod for Eaglercraft, letting you play on online Minecraft Java Edition servers in your browser.
Firefox WASM - A port of the Gecko engine to WebAssembly so that Firefox can be loaded inside another browser
wisp2socks - A client for Wisp that exposes the connection over a socks connection.

🪟 wland

Wayland apps, composited in the browser.

wland is a Wayland compositor compiled to WebAssembly, ~65 kB gzipped in total. Real apps like foot and nautilus speak the real wire protocol, unmodified, and show up as windows in a web page. Typing, menus, clipboard, drag and drop, HiDPI and window controls all work. ⚡ It's fast too: up to 120 FPS on a Retina MacBook.

👉 See it in action

Quick start · CLI · Docker · SDK · How it works · Relay · Security · What works · Limits · Building

🚀 Quick start

Run the demo image. It works anywhere Docker does:

docker run -it --rm -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/pithings/wland

Open http://localhost:8080. Chromium and the PCManFM file manager are running inside the container, and show up as windows in the page. Open the README.txt in the file manager for things to try.

In the page:

Drag a titlebar to move a window, or Alt+drag anywhere.
Drag an edge to resize.
Use the top bar to switch windows.
Alt+F9 minimizes, Alt+F10 maximizes, Alt+F11 goes fullscreen.

Only one tab is the desktop at a time. A newly opened tab takes over.

More on the image under Docker.

💻 CLI

To show the apps of your own machine, run the server directly. This needs Linux (unix sockets with fd passing):

npx wland

Open the printed URL in your browser. Then launch apps from any shell:

npx wland run foot        # terminal
npx wland run nautilus    # GTK file manager
npx wland run xterm       # X11 apps work too (needs xwayland-satellite)
wl-copy hello             # the clipboard is shared between apps

The commands:

wland [serve] [options]                     # start the server
wland run [--display NAME] <app> [args...]  # launch an app against it

Server options:

--port N — HTTP port (default 8080).
--host ADDR — address to listen on (default 127.0.0.1). See Security before widening it.
--display NAME — Wayland socket name. Default: the first free wayland-N.
--runtime-dir DIR — socket folder. Default: $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.
--xwayland auto|off|PATH — X11 apps through xwayland-satellite. auto uses it when installed.
--web-root DIR — serve your own page instead of the bundled one.

wland run sets everything an app needs: WAYLAND_DISPLAY, DISPLAY for X11, software rendering for GTK, and a session dbus if none is running.

You can also run apps directly. If the server got wayland-0, plain foot just works. Inside a desktop session it picks wayland-1 instead, and prints what to set. It never takes over a socket that is in use.

🐳 Docker

The demo image holds the server, its page, Chromium, PCManFM and a small text editor (l3afpad), for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

Pass the apps to run, one command line per argument (the default is chromium pcmanfm):

docker run -it --rm -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/pithings/wland "chromium https://example.org"

The apps keep running across a page reload or a closed tab: the image runs the server with --profile session, where the compositor lives in the server and the page shows it. An app you close stays closed until the next page load. -e WLAND_PROFILE=passthrough puts the compositor in the page instead; a reload then disconnects every app and they are started again.

There is no authentication, and -p 8080:8080 publishes the desktop on every address of your machine. On a network you don't trust, publish it on loopback only: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080.

To build the image yourself:

docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t wland .
📦 SDK

The bundled page is just one way to use wland. You can embed the compositor in your own page, or drive apps from a Node script.

npm install wland

The package has four entry points:

wland/client — the compositor for a web page.
wland/engine — the compositor without any DOM (Worker, Node).
wland/headless — a DOM-free desktop for scripts and tests.
wland — Node helpers to start the server and launch apps.
Embed in a page
import { createWland } from 'wland/client';

const wl = await createWland({
  container: document.getElementById('desktop'),
});

The container is the desktop. Give it a position and a fixed size: apps see its size as the screen. Wland owns its children, so put your own UI next to it, not inside.

By default it connects to /ws on the same host, which is what the server provides.

Build a taskbar
const wl = await createWland({
  container,
  onWindowsChange() {
    taskbar.replaceChildren(...wl.windows().map((w) => {
      const b = document.createElement('button');
      b.textContent = w.title;
      b.classList.toggle('active', w.focused);
      b.onclick = () => w.raise();   // focus, or restore if minimized
      return b;
    }));
  },
});

Each window also has appId (the app's set_app_id, e.g. for its icon), minimize(), restore(), setMaximized(on), setFullscreen(on) and close() (asks the app to close the window; the app decides, and may ask about unsaved work first).

Show connection status
const wl = await createWland({
  container,
  onEvent(ev) {
    if (ev.type === 'open') status.textContent = 'connected';
    if (ev.type === 'close') {
      status.textContent = ev.takenOver ? 'moved to another tab' : 'disconnected';
    }
  },
});

To reconnect, call wl.dispose() and then createWland() again. Dispose removes everything wland added, with no page reload.

More options
import { createWland, createWsLink } from 'wland/client';

await createWland({
  container,
  link: createWsLink('wss://example.com/ws'),  // a different relay
  scale: 2,                   // pin the scale, 1.5 works too (default: follows devicePixelRatio)
  webgl: 'never',             // 'auto' | 'always' | 'never'
  browserFullscreen: true,    // fullscreen windows also go browser-fullscreen
  shortcuts: false,           // turn off Alt+F9/F10/F11 ({ keys, drag }: the keys and Alt+drag apart)
  clipboard: false,           // keep the Wayland clipboard inside the desktop
});

See lib/client.ts for every option.

Clipboard

By default the Wayland clipboard and the page's clipboard are bridged, for plain text, both ways:

Paste into an app. Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Shift+V or Shift+Insert in the desktop makes the browser fire its paste event. wland makes that text the clipboard of the focused app before the key reaches it, so the app's own paste reads it. (The key waits for the event: Chromium sends it at once, Firefox a moment later.) The keys themselves reach the app unchanged: in a terminal Ctrl+C is still an interrupt and Ctrl+V literal-next (terminals paste with Ctrl+Shift+V). Ctrl+C in the desktop never copies what the page has selected.
Copy out of an app. When an app copies, wland reads the text and writes it to the page's clipboard while the browser allows that: right away if you pressed a key or clicked in the desktop within the last 5 seconds (Chromium, Firefox), otherwise at your next key or click in the desktop, or your next Ctrl+C there (Safari needs one of those).
macOS, iOS (not yet tried on a Mac or an iPad: see Current limits). Cmd+C, Cmd+X and Cmd+V are the chords there (Ctrl+V is no paste in a Mac browser: it goes to the app as a plain key). They reach the app as Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V, the chords Linux apps know, each sent whole when the chord is pressed (macOS browsers drop the key's release while Cmd is held); so in a terminal Cmd+V is literal-next and Cmd+C an interrupt — paste there with Cmd+Shift+V (Ctrl+Shift+V) where the browser makes it a paste, or Cmd+V once into any other app and then the terminal's Ctrl+Shift+V.

Which side is newer is decided by where you were. You are elsewhere once the desktop loses the keyboard focus (another tab or window, page UI, a click on plain page text) or you click outside it. An app that copies while you are elsewhere (a script's wl-copy, a background app) never writes the page clipboard while you are away; apps in the desktop paste its text. The first look wland gets at the page clipboard after you are back decides — your next paste in the desktop, or coming back itself if the browser has already granted clipboard-read: if the page clipboard is what wland last saw there, the app's text is newer — it is written to the page (and pasted); if it changed (you copied something meanwhile, text or not), yours stays and is pasted. An app clearing the clipboard (a password manager's timeout, wl-copy --clear) clears the page clipboard too while it still holds that app's text — when you are away, at that first look. An app that merely exits (or a dropped connection) leaves the page clipboard alone, as a clipboard manager would, and its text still pastes into the other apps from there.

It never reads the page's clipboard on its own, with one exception: if the browser has already granted clipboard-read to the page, focusing the desktop reads it, so an app's Paste menu sees what you copied elsewhere. An app sees the page's text only while it has keyboard focus. Text copied inside the desktop and pasted back in stays the app's (no round trip), and a page clipboard that is older than an app's copy never replaces it. Text over 4 MiB is not bridged. Other types (HTML, images) are not bridged yet; the engine API below carries any type. The bridge needs a relay that speaks it, and checks on every connection: in front of an older relay (wlandr 0.1.0) it switches itself off for that connection with one log line, and the copy and paste keys go to the apps as plain keys, as with clipboard: false; apps still copy and paste among themselves.

From code (both wland/engine and wland/headless):

import { readSelectionText, setSelectionText } from 'wland/engine';

await readSelectionText(engine);       // the app's clipboard as text, or null
setSelectionText(engine, 'hello');     // offer text to the focused app
engine.readSelection('image/png');     // any type, as bytes (Promise)
engine.setSelection({ 'text/html': '<b>hi</b>', 'text/plain': 'hi' });
// 'selection' events tell you when it changes: { conn, mimes }
// (an app's conn with no mimes: it cleared it; conn 0 with none: its owner went)
engine.selectionBridged();             // false on a relay too old for this:
// reads then reject (NO_SELECTION_BRIDGE) and setSelection returns false
Output size and scale

The output apps see follows the container's size (a ResizeObserver: if your layout resizes the container, apps get the new size) and the device pixel ratio, live. A hidden container (display: none) keeps the last size. To decide yourself after start, pin either one:

wl.output.setSize({ width: 1920, height: 1080 }); // apps see this, whatever the container
wl.output.setScale(1.5);                          // integer or fractional
wl.output.setSize(null);                          // follow the container again
wl.output.setScale(null);                         // follow devicePixelRatio again
wl.output.state();                                // { width, height, scale, sizePinned, scalePinned }

A size is rounded to whole px and each side must round to at least 1; a scale must be a finite number above 0. Anything else throws a RangeError and changes nothing (an invalid scale option rejects createWland, leaving nothing behind). After dispose() these calls do nothing.

Start the server from Node
import { startServer } from 'wland';

const server = await startServer({ port: 8080 });
console.log(server.url);      // open this in a browser
// server.process.kill() stops it
